newsitem.title: USA: Teamsters, UPS recess talks until noon Friday.
newsitem.headline: Teamsters, UPS recess talks until noon Friday.

text.p: The Teamsters union and United Parcel Service agreed to resume negotiations at noon (1600 GMT) on Friday after failing to end the strike affecting worldwide shipments at meetings Thursday.
"The ball, we think, is in their court," said Teamsters President Ron Carey as he left the talks at nearly 12:30 a.m. (0430 GMT) on Friday after 10-1/2 hours of bargaining.
Carey said there was no progress to end the strike by 185,000 union members but expressed hope the two sides could hammer out an agreement when they meet again.
"It's not rocket science," he said. "If the company is willing to agree and if the union is willing to look at their position, you can reach an agreement in 15 minutes."

The five-day strike has choked off the delivery of nearly 12 million packages daily across the United States. Some 90 units of blood products had to be destroyed because overnight delivery was delayed, a blood bank reported.
The company insisted publicly that it has no interest in changing its offer. But the two sides kept talking under the watchful eye of federal mediator John Calhoun Wells.

"We do have a last, best and final offer on the table," UPS Chairman James Kelly told reporters as he went into the talks Thursday afternoon. "We are perplexed and don't understand why the Teamsters won't let us send that out to our people." But he had nothing to say as he left the talks.
The Teamsters blamed the strike on the company's refusal to create more full-time jobs each year for the two-thirds of its union workers who are now part time.
UPS said the real issue was the Teamsters' refusal to let the company withdraw from a union pension plan that includes 30 other companies. UPS says running its own plan would save money.

As the strike continued, tensions were rising and some pickets were arrested. The company sought court orders in Ohio, Massachusetts, California, Colorado, New York and other states to prevent striking workers from blocking delivery trucks and managers from reporting to work.
A state court in Colorado granted a 10-day order limiting the number of pickets.
A prolonged strike could damage the economy, Federal Reserve Governor Susan Phillips said Thursday. "If it goes on for a long time, we'll start to see some economic impact," she told Reuters.
But she added: "I'm not too worried at this point."
The union estimated UPS was losing $35 million daily in profits. UPS spokeswoman Gina Ellrich said the company had no precise estimate, but that it was losing "tens of millions of dollars a day."
Even if there is no progress at the talks, the two sides may be reluctant to leave them after President Clinton and Labour Secretary Alexis Herman pushed them to begin again.
Since the strike began, UPS has been handling less than 10 percent of its normal shipments, using 50,000 non-union employees to do the work of striking loaders, sorters and drivers.
The company has 300,000 workers, more than 200,000 represented by the union, although not all are members.
